name: Gastilonys Oak
species_basis: genus commonly used generically in Lithuanian registers; presumed robur as the dominant native oak, not itemised explicitly in either source

location.address: Kauno marių regioninis parkas (Kaunas Reservoir Regional Park), beside the Gastilionys outcrop (Gastilionių atodanga), Rumšiškės eldership, Kaišiadorys district

access: Free; stands in the public Kauno marių Regional Park, reached via signposted paths at the start of the Gastilionys outcrop gorge, a public geological viewpoint
transport: Kaišiadorys district, about 16km east of central Kaunas by road toward Rumšiškės; no public transit stop found this pass, reachable by car as a day-trip addition to Kaunas
story:
A tourism guide for the Kaišiadorys district calls this the thickest tree in the whole of Kaunas Reservoir Regional Park, and it grows at the mouth of one of the park's sights. The Gastilionys outcrop is a cliff and gorge cut into the valley, a geological viewpoint people come to see on its own account. The oak stands where the path into that gorge begins.

The two sources that describe it do not quite agree on its size, and the reason is where they held the tape. The district guide gives 5.25 metres round and 21 metres tall. The state cadastre, as Lithuanian Wikipedia reports it, gives 5.50 metres and 25 metres, but measured at the base of the trunk rather than at chest height, which always reads fatter. Either way it is a big oak.

It grows in mixed forest beside an old logging clearing, and the guide singles out its symmetrical branching, a crown built to take the strong winds that come off the reservoir. It has been protected as state natural heritage since 2008. The sources call it an oak without naming the species; pedunculate oak is the likely one, as the country's dominant native, but nobody has said so in writing.

It is about 16 kilometres east of central Kaunas by road, toward Rumšiškės, and easiest by car. Nobody has published its age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad, evenly branched crown on a trunk about 5.25 metres round. It stands in mixed forest at the start of the path into the Gastilionys outcrop gorge.

name: The Plokščiai Oak (Panemunė)

location.address: Beside the 'Kentėjimo kelias' (Suffering Path) memorial, near road 3807 (Kiduliai-Gelgaudiškis-Gerdžiūnai), Plokščiai village, on the south bank of the Nemunas within Panemunių Regional Park, Šakiai district

access: Free; stands on public land within Panemunių Regional Park, beside a public road and a memorial site
transport: Šakiai district, about 2.8km from Raudonė (Jurbarkas district) by road, on the opposite side of the Nemunas within the same regional park; reachable by car, no public transit checked this pass
story:
Children in Plokščiai used to climb inside this oak. The base of the trunk rotted out long ago, leaving a hollow big enough to play in, and people who grew up in the village still remember doing it.

The hollow has not stopped it growing. It stands 34 metres tall, which is a great deal for an oak. The trunk is 5.2 metres round.

For all that, it had no official status until very recently. Lithuania's Environment Ministry designated it only in September 2025, in the same order that protected a wave of other big oaks across the country, including the Netoniai oak outside Kaunas. It is one of the eleven natural heritage objects of Panemunių Regional Park, the stretch of the Nemunas valley famous for its castles.

It grows on the south bank of the river, beside the Kentėjimo kelias, the Suffering Path memorial, near the road through Plokščiai village. That puts it about 2.8 kilometres by road from the Castle Lime at Raudonė on the far side of the valley, close enough to make the two a single outing. There is another Plokščiai oak in Kretinga district, near Klaipėda; this is not it.

Nobody has published an age for this tree. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its great height, 34 metres, above a trunk 5.2 metres round and hollow at the base. It stands beside the Kentėjimo kelias memorial by the road through Plokščiai, across the Nemunas from Raudonė.

name: Ilguva Oak

location.address: About 130m south of Ilguva Church, within the Nykos landscape reserve, Ilguva village, Kriūkai eldership, Šakiai district

access: Free, but genuinely hard to find: no gate or ownership restriction, but the tree stands off any marked path, reached by walking along the Nyka stream from Dulinčiškiai village (in Panemunė) and climbing a slope
transport: Šakiai district; about 12.7km from Raudonė by road, no public transit checked this pass
story:
This is the oak you have to look for. It stands off any marked path on a slope in the Nykos landscape reserve, and the usual way in is on foot along the Nyka stream from the village of Dulinčiškiai, then up the bank. The pin gets you close; the last stretch is yours.

What you find is worth the scramble. The trunk is 5.42 metres round at chest height, measured in 2014, and at 3.8 metres it splits into three stems that carry the tree to 32 metres. The crown alone is 22 metres tall and 22 metres wide, as broad as it is deep.

The state cadastre puts it at 300 to 400 years old. That range is the register's own, not something we worked out, and it has been protected since 2005. Even the low end means this oak was already growing on its slope when the Nemunas valley below was still part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

It is 12.7 kilometres from Raudonė by road, a longer detour than the Plokščiai oak across the river, and best treated as a small expedition of its own; Ilguva's church, about 130 metres to the north, is the landmark to aim for. Everything here rests on one published source, the cadastre as Lithuanian Wikipedia reports it. If you find the tree, a photograph and a word about the way in would help the next person.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.42 metres round, splitting into three stems at 3.8 metres under a crown 22 metres wide. It stands off the paths on a slope above the Nyka stream, about 130 metres south of Ilguva Church.

name: Šilalė Independence Oak

location.address: Traffic island at the J. Basanavičiaus / Nepriklausomybės street intersection, central Šilalė

access: Free; public street island in the town centre, no gate or fee, though it stands amid busy traffic
transport: Central Šilalė, walkable from anywhere in town; the closest bus stops serve regional routes
story:
The stones at the foot of this oak carry a single date, 1918-02-16, the day Lithuania declared its independence. The tree was planted to mark an anniversary of it. Which anniversary is still argued over in Šilalė.

The local historian Kazimieras Šetkus put the planting in 1937, for the twentieth. Another account puts it in 1927 or 1928, for the tenth. That leaves the oak somewhere between 89 and 99 years old, young by the standards of this map and chosen for what it stands for rather than its size: 2.40 metres round and 15 metres tall.

What it has lived through is the point. Planted as a symbol of a young state, it stood through the Soviet decades when that date could not be celebrated, and was still there when it could be again. The town made it a natural heritage object in 2006.

Its enemy now is traffic. It grows on an island in the middle of a busy junction, and road salt and passing lorries have been hard on it. Since 2018 the municipality has been nursing it back: replacing the soil, mulching the roots, pulling out old wire, and shielding it from salt each winter.

It is the first stop of an afternoon in Šilalė. The memorial grove for 13 January 1991 stands 90 metres away across the same junction, and two far bigger oaks wait in the countryside around Kaltinėnai, 16 kilometres out.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stones at its base inscribed 1918-02-16, on an oak 2.40 metres round and 15 metres tall. It stands on the traffic island at the Basanavičiaus and Nepriklausomybės junction.

name: Oaks and Lime of January 13
species: Oak (Quercus sp., x13) and Lime (Tilia sp., x1)
species_basis: genus read from lt.wikipedia's description of the memorial grove; individual species per tree not itemised in the source

location.address: J. Basanavičiaus / Nepriklausomybės street intersection, around the 'Laisvės šauklys' (Freedom's Crier) sculpture, central Šilalė

access: Free; public street-corner plot with benches, no gate or fee, genuinely reachable
transport: Central Šilalė, about 90m from the Independence Oak, walkable
story:
Count the trees and you have the dead. Thirteen oaks and one lime stand in a semicircle on this street corner, one for each of the thirteen men and one woman killed when Soviet troops stormed the Vilnius television tower on 13 January 1991.

That night is the hinge of modern Lithuanian history. Unarmed civilians had gathered around the tower and the parliament to defend the independence declared the previous March, and the deaths hardened resistance at home and opinion abroad. Within a year Moscow had recognised the country.

Šilalė's memorial is small and exact. The trees ring a sculpture by Kazimieras Kisielis, Laisvės šauklys, Freedom's Crier: thirteen oaks and a single lime for thirteen men and a single woman. There are benches, and the whole plot covers about a fifth of a hectare. The town declared it a natural heritage object in 2006.

These are young trees, and nobody pretends otherwise. No planting date has been published for them, but they most likely went in with the monument during the 1990s, which makes them roughly 30 to 35 years old. They are here for what they mean, not for their girth, and nobody has measured them one by one.

The Independence Oak stands 90 metres away at the same junction, so the two memorials make one stop: a tree for the state founded in 1918, and fourteen for the people who died to restore it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the semicircle of thirteen oaks and one lime ringing the Freedom's Crier sculpture, with benches. It stands at the Basanavičiaus and Nepriklausomybės junction, 90 metres from the Independence Oak.

name: Laumenai Oak

location.address: Off the old Žemaičių Highway, roughly midway between Laukuva and Kaltinėnai, via Bilioniai village, Laumenai village, Kaltinėnai eldership, Šilalė district

access: No gate or ownership restriction stated in the source, but genuinely remote: stands amid cultivated fields and pastures in hilly farmland, described as hard to spot from nearby roads
transport: Šilalė district, about 16-18km from central Šilalė and about 6.5km from Pundžiai Oak (below); reachable by car only, no public transit checked this pass
story:
A small chapel hangs on the side of this oak, the same side where lightning tore into it. The scar runs from about eight metres up into the crown, the chapel is in poor repair, and the tree is still standing over both.

There is more at ground level: a small cave has opened beneath the roots. Between the strike, the shrine and the hollow underneath, this is a tree that has been through things, and it shows all of them at once.

It is a pedunculate oak 4.9 metres round at chest height, or 4.8 by the state registry's own count, and 17 metres tall, or 15 by the registry. The crown measures 17 metres and the first branches start four and a half metres up. It has been protected since 2005.

Getting there is part of it. The oak stands among cultivated fields and pastures in hilly farmland off the old Žemaičių Highway, roughly midway between Laukuva and Kaltinėnai, reached through the village of Bilioniai. The source warns it is hard to spot from the nearby roads, so trust the pin, which is tree-level, and look across the fields. It is 16 to 18 kilometres from central Šilalė by car, and 6.5 kilometres from the Pundžiai oak, which makes the two one drive.

Everything here rests on one published source, and nobody has dated the tree. If you know its age, or how the chapel came to be there, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small chapel on its lightning-scarred side and the cave beneath its roots, on a trunk 4.9 metres round. It stands among fields and pasture near Laumenai, off the old Žemaičių Highway.

name: Pundžiai Oak

location.address: Pundžiai forest, about 3km west of Kaltinėnai, 50m south of the old Žemaičių Highway, Rietavas Forest Management District, Šilalė district

access: Free; state forest under Rietavas Forest Management District, no ownership restriction, though as of a 2020 note the surrounding undergrowth was dense and the old fencing deteriorated, complicating (not preventing) a visit
transport: Šilalė district, about 16km from central Šilalė and about 6.5km from Laumenai Oak (above); reachable by car only, no public transit checked this pass
story:
At 33.5 metres, this oak is more than twice the height of the Independence Oak in town, and at 5.6 metres round it is the thickest of the four trees on this page. Oaks rarely get this tall.

It stands in Pundžiai forest, about three kilometres west of Kaltinėnai and only 50 metres south of the old Žemaičių Highway, the historic road across Samogitia. Lithuania declared it a protected monument in 1989, in the last years of Soviet rule, and it is now looked after by the Rietavas state forest district.

The record on it is plain and administrative: measurements, a designation, and some honest notes on its condition. Animals have dug burrows under the roots. The canopy has been observed to be thinning. By 2020 the old fence around it had fallen into disrepair and the undergrowth had grown dense, which makes the last 50 metres slower than they look on a map without stopping anyone. None of that says it is dying, but it is not a tree in its prime either, and a photograph from anyone who visits would tell us how it is doing now.

It is about 16 kilometres from central Šilalė by car and 6.5 kilometres from the Laumenai oak, so the two countryside oaks make one drive. Nobody has published its age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 33.5 metres, on a trunk 5.6 metres round inside an old, broken fence. It stands in Pundžiai forest, 50 metres south of the old Žemaičių Highway, three kilometres west of Kaltinėnai.

name: The Vepriai Oak

location.address: Beside the Veprių Kalvarijos (Way of the Cross) path, about 20m southeast of the third station chapel, Deltuva forestry unit, Vepriai village, Ukmergė district
location.neighbourhood: Vepriai, beside the Veprių Kalvarijos pilgrimage path

access: Free; stands in state forest directly beside a public pilgrimage path with an information marker installed as of autumn 2025
transport: Ukmergė district; no public transit stop checked this pass, reachable by car; Ukmergė town itself is not currently a published place
story:
The pilgrims come for the Stations of the Cross, and the oak is waiting for them at the third one. Vepriai's Kalvarijos is a Way of the Cross five and a half kilometres long, with 35 stations strung through forest, across meadow and along a lakeshore, and this tree stands 20 metres from the chapel of the third.

The path was laid out in 1846. The brick chapels came later, between 1882 and 1900, and it was the local farmers who paid for them. At Whitsun it drew crowds: in the years between the wars, thousands of people walked it. It is still a living pilgrimage route, not a museum piece.

The oak is not the reason the path exists, and it does not need to be. It is 30 metres tall, a real height for an oak, and 4.30 metres round at chest height. Lithuania protected it in 2016, and in autumn 2025 an information marker went up beside it, so you will not have to guess which trunk it is.

That is the way to see it: walk the Kalvarijos, or at least its first stretch, and stop at the third chapel. The oak is one marked feature on a route through a landscape that people have been walking on purpose for 180 years.

It is in the Ukmergė district, easiest by car. The facts on the tree come from a single register entry, and nobody has published its age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the information marker beside it and its height, 30 metres on a trunk 4.30 metres round. It stands on the Kalvarijos path, about 20 metres southeast of the third station chapel.

name: The Žadeikoniai Oak

location.address: On a hillock within the old Oniūnai cemetery, about 5km southwest of Saločiai near road 3116 (Saločiai-Telžiai), Žadeikoniai village, Saločiai eldership, Pasvalys district

access: Free; a small, fenced village cemetery with gates, no fee; reachable near a bridge over the Kamatis stream, visible from it
transport: Pasvalys district; no public transit stop checked this pass, reachable by car; Pasvalys town is not currently a published place
story:
This oak was protected by the state on 1 September 1960, one of the first trees in Lithuania to be given that status, and it has spent its life among the dead. It stands on a hillock inside the old Oniūnai cemetery, a small fenced village graveyard in the countryside southwest of Saločiai.

It earns the trip on size. The trunk is 6.05 metres round at chest height, close behind the biggest Lithuanian oaks on this map, the Gudlaukis oak at 6.30 metres among them, and the crown rises to 22 metres.

The ground here has had its own surprises. In January 2009 a sinkhole seven metres across opened in the ground near the oak. It was filled, and the tree carried on.

Its age is a small mystery of its own. The state cadastre lists the field as not disclosed, which is not the same as unknown: somebody may hold a figure and has chosen not to publish it. We have not been able to find one anywhere else. If you know how old it is, tell us.

The cemetery has gates and costs nothing to enter. It lies about five kilometres southwest of Saločiai, near road 3116 toward Telžiai, by a bridge over the Kamatis stream, and the oak is visible from the bridge. You will need a car; there is nothing else on this map nearby, and this tree is the reason to come.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.05 metres round, on a hillock inside the fenced old Oniūnai cemetery. It stands near the bridge over the Kamatis stream, and you can see it from the bridge.
